meta: Free electrical converters for watts, amps, volts, kW, kVA, VA and amp hours. Each tool shows the formula with your numbers for DC, single and three phase.
author: ali-ahmad

p: To find the current an appliance draws, use the watts to amps calculator; for a battery or solar circuit, the twelve-volt watts to amps calculator; for mains in Pakistan, the watts to amps calculator for a home supply. To go the other way, from the amps on a meter or clamp to power, use amps to watts, amps to kW or, with the voltage you measured, volts to watts.

Generators and UPS units are rated in kVA or VA, not watts: the kVA to kW calculator and the VA to watts calculator give the real power they can carry. Batteries are rated in amp hours; the Ah to Wh calculator turns that into the energy they store. For a three-phase connection use the three-phase amps calculator.

l.t: watts to amps calculator for a home supply

p: On AC mains, watts = volts × amps × power factor. A heater or kettle has a power factor of one, but motors, compressors and electronics draw some current that does no work, so a mixed home load is planned at 0.8 and a generator at 0.8. On a DC battery there is no power factor: the amps are simply the watts divided by the volts.

faq.q: How do I convert watts to amps?
faq.a: Divide the watts by the volts; on AC mains also divide by the power factor, and on three-phase by √3 × the line voltage instead. The watts to amps calculator does it for DC, single-phase and three-phase supplies and shows each step.

faq.q: Is kVA the same as kW?
faq.a: No. kVA is apparent power and kW is real power: kW = kVA × power factor. At the usual generator power factor a set delivers about 80% of its kVA rating as kW, which is why a generator or UPS label overstates the load it can carry.

faq.q: Which voltage should I use for Pakistan?
faq.a: 230 V for a single-phase home and 400 V between lines for a three-phase connection, at fifty hertz. Older labels may give a slightly lower nominal voltage; the difference in amps is small.

faq.q: How do I find the watt hours of a battery?
faq.a: Multiply its amp hours by its voltage. Only part of that energy is usable: about 50% for a tubular battery and 90% for lithium, which the battery and UPS calculators apply for you.

key_facts: Amps = watts ÷ (volts × power factor). On a 230 V single-phase supply, 1,500 W at a power factor of 0.8 draws 8.15 A.
kW = kVA × power factor, so at the usual generator power factor of 0.8 every kVA gives 0.8 kW of real power.
Watt hours = amp hours × volts, so a 200 Ah 12 V battery stores 2,400 Wh (2.4 kWh) and a 100 Ah 12 V battery stores 1,200 Wh (1.2 kWh).

content.answer: These converters turn one electrical unit into another: watts to amps, amps to watts, kW and kVA, VA to watts and amp hours to watt hours. Pick the supply first, a DC battery, single-phase or three-phase mains, because the same watts draw very different amps on each. Every result shows the formula with your numbers.
